claim: Microorganisms constantly transition between environments with dramatically different external osmolarities.
source: Microorganisms constantly transition between environments with dramatically different external osmolarities.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on microbial osmoresponse.

claim: Upon a hypoosmotic shock, the turgor pressure increases immediately due to the sudden water influx.
source: Upon a hypoosmotic shock (i.e. a sudden decrease of the external osmolarity), the turgor pressure increases immediately due to the sudden water influx.
evidence: Based on established understanding of osmotic responses and cited literature.

claim: To relax the turgor pressure, the cell upregulates the cell-wall synthesis rate, adds more materials to the peptidoglycan network, and eventually adapts to the lower external osmolarity.
source: To relax the turgor pressure, the cell upregulates the cell-wall synthesis rate, adds more materials to the peptidoglycan network, and eventually adapts to the lower external osmolarity (Typas et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Typas et al., 2010.

claim: Upon a hyperosmotic shock, the cell volume of a microbial cell shrinks within milliseconds due to water efflux, leading to a decreased turgor pressure.
source: Upon a hyperosmotic shock (i.e. a sudden increase of the external osmolarity), the cell volume of a microbial cell shrinks within milliseconds due to water efflux, leading to a decreased turgor pressure (Rojas and Huang, 2018; Cadart et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rojas and Huang, 2018 and Cadart et al., 2019.

claim: To increase the internal osmotic pressure, microorganisms increase their intracellular solute pool by amassing osmolyte molecules through de novo synthesis.
source: To increase the internal osmotic pressure, microorganisms increase their intracellular solute pool by amassing osmolyte molecules (i.e. osmoregulation), e.g., through de novo synthesis (Kempf and Bremer, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kempf and Bremer, 1998.

claim: Intracellular crowding may act as a cell volume sensor to trigger osmoregulation.
source: Intracellular crowding may act as a cell volume sensor to trigger osmoregulation (Burg, 2000; van den Berg et al., 2017; Model et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burg, 2000; van den Berg et al., 2017; Model et al., 2021.

claim: Intracellular crowding due to volume reduction inevitably affects the cellular physiology globally, e.g., slowing down protein diffusion.
source: Meanwhile, intracellular crowding due to volume reduction inevitably affects the cellular physiology globally, e.g., slowing down protein diffusion (Dix and Verkman, 2008; Dill et al., 2011; Miermont et al., 2013; Mika et al., 2014; Munder et al., 2016; Joyner et al., 2016; Molines et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting effects of crowding on protein diffusion.

claim: Intracellular crowding reduces the elongation speed of translating ribosomes.
source: Meanwhile, intracellular crowding due to volume reduction inevitably affects the cellular physiology globally, e.g., slowing down protein diffusion (Dix and Verkman, 2008; Dill et al., 2011; Miermont et al., 2013; Mika et al., 2014; Munder et al., 2016; Joyner et al., 2016; Molines et al., 2022) and reducing the elongation speed of translating ribosomes (Dai et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dai et al., 2018 and Chen et al., 2023.

claim: Microbial cells can adapt to a broad range of external osmolarity, with the external osmotic pressure varying over an order of magnitude.
source: For example, it is widely observed that microbial cells can adapt to a broad range of external osmolarity, with the external osmotic pressure varying over an order of magnitude (Cayley et al., 1991; Dai et al., 2018; Rojas et al., 2014; Rojas et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting osmotic adaptation ranges.

claim: The growth rate in the steady state decreases as the external osmolarity increases.
source: Furthermore, the growth rate in the steady state decreases as the external osmolarity increases, and a complete arrest of cell growth occurs above a critical osmolarity (Scott, 1953; Christian and Scott, 1953; Christian, 1955; Rojas et al., 2014; Rojas et al., 2017; Dai et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting growth rate dependence on osmolarity.

claim: A complete arrest of cell growth occurs above a critical osmolarity.
source: Furthermore, the growth rate in the steady state decreases as the external osmolarity increases, and a complete arrest of cell growth occurs above a critical osmolarity (Scott, 1953; Christian and Scott, 1953; Christian, 1955; Rojas et al., 2014; Rojas et al., 2017; Dai et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting critical osmolarity for growth arrest.

claim: An overshoot of growth rate often occurs upon a hypoosmotic shock.
source: Moreover, upon an osmotic shock, the growth rate usually does not approach the new steady-state value monotonically, e.g., an overshoot of growth rate often occurs upon a hypoosmotic shock (Rojas et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rojas et al., 2017.

claim: A damped oscillation of growth rate can happen after a hyperosmotic shock.
source: Moreover, upon an osmotic shock, the growth rate usually does not approach the new steady-state value monotonically, e.g., an overshoot of growth rate often occurs upon a hypoosmotic shock (Rojas et al., 2017), and a damped oscillation of growth rate can happen after a hyperosmotic shock (Rojas et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rojas et al., 2014.

claim: In experiments of Schizosaccharomyces pombe by Knapp et al., 2019, an oscillatory osmotic shock was applied to cells, during which cell volume growth was dramatically slowed down while biomass was still actively produced.
source: In recent experiments of Schizosaccharomyces pombe by Knapp et al., 2019, an oscillatory osmotic shock was applied to cells, during which cell volume growth was dramatically slowed down while biomass was still actively produced.
evidence: Directly references experimental observations from Knapp et al., 2019.

claim: A supergrowth phase happened after removing the oscillatory osmotic shock, during which cells grew much faster than the steady state before the shocks.
source: Surprisingly, a supergrowth phase happened after removing the oscillatory osmotic shock, during which cells grew much faster than the steady state before the shocks.
evidence: Describes experimental observation from Knapp et al., 2019.

claim: The change in free water volume within the cell is driven by osmotic imbalance.
source: Our model assumes the following phenomenological rules: (1) the change in free water volume within the cell is driven by osmotic imbalance (Cadart et al., 2019; Rollin et al., 2023)
evidence: Model assumption supported by citations to Cadart et al., 2019 and Rollin et al., 2023.

claim: The remaining volume changes in proportion to protein production.
source: Our model assumes the following phenomenological rules: (1) the change in free water volume within the cell is driven by osmotic imbalance (Cadart et al., 2019; Rollin et al., 2023), while the remaining volume changes in proportion to protein production
evidence: Model assumption based on theoretical framework.

claim: Osmoregulation influences the production of osmolyte-producing protein, governed by intracellular protein density.
source: (2) osmoregulation influences the production of osmolyte-producing protein, governed by intracellular protein density
evidence: Model assumption based on theoretical framework.

claim: Cell-wall synthesis is regulated through a feedback mechanism, wherein turgor pressure modulates the efficiency of cell-wall synthesis, enabling the cell to maintain a relatively stable turgor pressure.
source: (3) cell-wall synthesis is regulated through a feedback mechanism, wherein turgor pressure modulates the efficiency of cell-wall synthesis, enabling the cell to maintain a relatively stable turgor pressure
evidence: Model assumption based on theoretical framework and cited literature.

claim: Intracellular crowding slows down biochemical reactions as the protein density increases, with reactions ceasing entirely when the protein density reaches a critical threshold.
source: (4) intracellular crowding slows down biochemical reactions as the protein density increases, with reactions ceasing entirely when the protein density reaches a critical threshold.
evidence: Model assumption based on theoretical framework and understanding of crowding effects.

claim: Upon a hyperosmotic shock, cell volume reduction due to water efflux increases the protein density, inducing the upregulation of osmolyte-producing protein but slowing down the translation speed due to crowding.
source: Upon a hyperosmotic shock, cell volume reduction due to water efflux increases the protein density, inducing the upregulation of osmolyte-producing protein but slowing down the translation speed due to crowding.
evidence: Inference from model assumptions and known biological responses.

claim: Upon a hypoosmotic shock, the dramatic water influx stretches the cell wall, and the increased turgor pressure induces cell-wall synthesis.
source: Upon a hypoosmotic shock, the dramatic water influx stretches the cell wall, and the increased turgor pressure induces cell-wall synthesis (Typas et al., 2010; Jiang and Sun, 2010; Amir and Nelson, 2012).
evidence: Inference from model assumptions supported by citations.

claim: The predicted steady-state growth rate as a function of internal osmotic pressure from the model aligns well with experimental data from diverse organisms.
source: Notably, the predicted steady-state growth rate as a function of internal osmotic pressure from our model aligns well with experimental data from diverse organisms.
evidence: Comparison between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: Osmoregulation and cell-wall synthesis regulation enable cells to adapt to a wide range of external osmolarities and prevent plasmolysis.
source: Additionally, we demonstrate that osmoregulation and cell-wall synthesis regulation enable cells to adapt to a wide range of external osmolarities and prevent plasmolysis.
evidence: Demonstrated through model analysis and simulations.

claim: The model predicts a non-monotonic time dependence of growth rate and protein density as they approach steady-state values following a constant osmotic shock.
source: Our model also predicts a non-monotonic time dependence of growth rate and protein density as they approach steady-state values following a constant osmotic shock, in concert with experimental observations (Rojas et al., 2014; Rojas et al., 2017).
evidence: Model prediction consistent with cited experimental observations.

claim: A supergrowth phase can arise following a sudden decrease in external osmolarity, driven by cell-wall synthesis regulation.
source: Moreover, we show that a supergrowth phase can arise following a sudden decrease in external osmolarity, driven by cell-wall synthesis regulation, either through the direct application of a hypoosmotic shock or the withdrawal of an oscillatory stimulus.
evidence: Model prediction based on theoretical analysis.

claim: The predicted amplitudes of supergrowth (i.e. growth rate peaks) quantitatively agree with multiple independent experimental measurements.
source: Remarkably, the predicted amplitudes of supergrowth (i.e. growth rate peaks) quantitatively agree with multiple independent experimental measurements (Knapp et al., 2019).
evidence: Quantitative comparison between model predictions and experimental data from Knapp et al., 2019.

claim: In the limit of an extreme hyperosmotic shock, the remaining cytoplasmic volume is comparable to the volume of expelled water.
source: In the limit of an extreme hyperosmotic shock, the remaining cytoplasmic volume is comparable to the volume of expelled water (Cayley et al., 1991; Scott Cayley et al., 2000; Miermont et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: The total cytoplasmic volume must be divided into a free volume and a bound volume.
source: Thus, the total cytoplasmic volume must be divided into a free volume and a bound volume (Whatmore and Reed, 1990; Cayley and Record, 2003; Lemière and Chang, 2023; Zhou et al., 2009; Rollin et al., 2023)
evidence: Model assumption supported by citations to literature.

claim: The cell-wall strain was measured by applying an acute hyperosmotic shock to induce plasmolysis, and it is approximately constant as the external osmolarity increases.
source: Experimentally, the cell-wall strain was measured by applying an acute hyperosmotic shock to induce plasmolysis, and it is approximately constant as the external osmolarity increases (Misra et al., 2013; Rojas et al., 2014), suggesting a constant turgor pressure independent of external osmolarity, in concert with our model assumptions.
evidence: Experimental observation from cited literature.

claim: Constant cell-wall strain as external osmolarity increases suggests a constant turgor pressure independent of external osmolarity.
source: Experimentally, the cell-wall strain was measured by applying an acute hyperosmotic shock to induce plasmolysis, and it is approximately constant as the external osmolarity increases (Misra et al., 2013; Rojas et al., 2014), suggesting a constant turgor pressure independent of external osmolarity, in concert with our model assumptions.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations and model predictions.

claim: The osmoadaptation capability of E. coli depends on the growth media, presumably arising from variations in metabolic fluxes and gene expressions.
source: Meanwhile, the osmoadaptation capability of E. coli depends on the growth media, presumably arising from variations in metabolic fluxes and gene expressions (Cayley et al., 1991; Dai et al., 2018; Rojas et al., 2014).
evidence: Observation from experimental data with speculative explanation.

claim: The steady-state growth curve of mutant cells without osmoregulation terminates at an external osmolarity much smaller than wild-type cells.
source: Therefore, the steady-state growth curve of the mutant cells terminates at an external osmolarity much smaller than wild-type (WT) cells (Figure 2B), in agreement with previous experiments (Brewster et al., 1993).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 2B and consistent with cited experiments.

claim: For mutant cells without cell-wall synthesis regulation, the turgor pressure at steady states decreases with the increase of external osmolarity.
source: Interestingly, in this case, the turgor pressure at steady states decreases with the increase of external osmolarity (Figure 2C and see the detailed proof in Section C of Appendix 1).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 2C with detailed proof in appendix.

claim: Mutant cells without cell-wall synthesis regulation grow faster than WT cells under the same external osmolarity.
source: Therefore, mutant cells grow faster than WT cells under the same external osmolarity (Figure 2B).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mutant cells without cell-wall synthesis regulation are prone to plasmolysis at a threshold external osmolarity where the WT cells can maintain constant turgor pressure.
source: Nevertheless, the mutant cells are prone to plasmolysis at a threshold external osmolarity where the WT cells can maintain constant turgor pressure (see the vertical line in Figure 2C around 2 M extra external osmolarity).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Reduced turgor pressure is detrimental to multiple biological processes, e.g., cytokinesis in fission yeast requires the participation of turgor pressure.
source: Reduced turgor pressure is detrimental to multiple biological processes, e.g., cytokinesis in fission yeast requires the participation of turgor pressure (Proctor et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Proctor et al., 2012.

claim: Osmoregulation allows cells to grow in a wide range of external osmolarity conditions with a mild change in protein density.
source: To summarize, osmoregulation allows cells to grow in a wide range of external osmolarity conditions with a mild change in protein density.
evidence: Summary conclusion from model analysis.

claim: Cell-wall synthesis regulation allows cells to maintain a stable turgor pressure and avoid plasmolysis.
source: The cell-wall synthesis regulation allows cells to maintain a stable turgor pressure and avoid plasmolysis.
evidence: Summary conclusion from model analysis.

claim: Both osmoregulation and cell-wall synthesis regulation expand the range of external osmolarities that cells can adapt to.
source: Both regulatory mechanisms expand the range of external osmolarities that cells can adapt to.
evidence: Summary conclusion from model analysis.

claim: The dynamics of osmoresponse can be split into shock and adaptation periods.
source: Intriguingly, we find that the dynamics of osmoresponse can be split into shock and adaptation periods (see insets of Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Model prediction illustrated in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The immediate water flow due to osmotic imbalance occurs in the shock period, during which the mass and osmolyte productions are negligible.
source: The immediate water flow due to osmotic imbalance occurs in the shock period, during which the mass and osmolyte productions are negligible.
evidence: Model assumption based on timescale separation.

claim: The timescale of osmoregulation is set by the doubling time: it takes about the doubling time for the protein density and the fraction of osmolyte-producing protein to adapt to the new steady-state values.
source: From the above equations, it is clear that the timescale of osmoregulation is set by the doubling time: it takes about the doubling time for the protein density and the fraction of osmolyte-producing protein to adapt to the new steady-state values.
evidence: Derived from model equations 12a and 12b.

claim: Upon a constant hyperosmotic shock, the immediate water efflux leads to an instantaneous drop in turgor pressure and a rise in protein density.
source: Upon a constant hyperosmotic shock, the immediate water efflux leads to an instantaneous drop in turgor pressure and a rise in protein density (Figure 3A).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The protein density increases initially and then decreases after a hyperosmotic shock.
source: Interestingly, the protein density increases initially and then decreases after the shock (Figure 3A).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The decrease in protein density after a hyperosmotic shock is because of the osmoregulation process, which is set by the doubling time.
source: The decrease in protein density is because of the osmoregulation process, which is set by the doubling time (Equation 12a and Equation 12b).
evidence: Explanation based on model dynamics.

claim: The initial increase of protein density after a hyperosmotic shock is because of the suppressed growth of the relaxed cell-wall volume due to the low turgor pressure.
source: Meanwhile, we find that the initial increase of protein density is because of the suppressed growth of the relaxed cell-wall volume due to the low turgor pressure.
evidence: Explanation based on model dynamics.

claim: The growth rate approaches the new steady-state value non-monotonically after a hyperosmotic shock.
source: We note that the growth rate approaches the new steady-state value non-monotonically (Figure 3A) because of the spiral trajectory in the space of the internal state (Figure 3C), consistent with experimental observations from Rojas et al., 2014.
evidence: Model prediction shown in Figure 3A and 3C, consistent with cited experiments.

claim: Extremely fast cell growth occurs after a hypoosmotic shock, with a growth rate peak occurring about 25 min after applying the shock.
source: However, we find extremely fast cell growth after the hypoosmotic shock, with a growth rate peak occurring about 25 min after applying the shock, which we call the supergrowth phase (Knapp et al., 2019).
evidence: Model prediction with timing consistent with experimental observations.

claim: Applying a hypoosmotic shock to an unwalled cell does not induce a significant supergrowth phase compared with walled cells.
source: Furthermore, applying a hypoosmotic shock to an unwalled cell does not induce a significant supergrowth phase compared with walled cells (Appendix 1—figure 2D).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Appendix 1—figure 2D.

claim: Supergrowth comes from the high turgor pressure caused by the hypoosmotic shock, which leads to fast cell-wall synthesis.
source: We propose that supergrowth comes from the high turgor pressure caused by the hypoosmotic shock, which leads to fast cell-wall synthesis according to Equation 7.
evidence: Mechanistic explanation based on model equations.

claim: Rapid insertion of materials into the cell wall relaxes the turgor pressure and allows the cells to grow faster.
source: Rapid insertion of materials into the cell wall relaxes the turgor pressure and allows the cells to grow faster (Equation 2 and Equation 3).
evidence: Mechanistic explanation based on model equations.

claim: The growth rate peak must increase as the amplitude of the hypoosmotic shock increases.
source: Therefore, the growth rate peak must increase as the amplitude of the hypoosmotic shock increases, which we confirm numerically in Figure 3E.
evidence: Model prediction confirmed by numerical simulations shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Knapp et al., 2019, applied an osmotic oscillation to fission yeast S. pombe during which the external osmolarity alternated between two values.
source: Knapp et al., 2019, applied an osmotic oscillation to fission yeast S. pombe during which the external osmolarity alternated between two values.
evidence: Description of experimental protocol from cited paper.

claim: Cell growth was almost inhibited during the osmotic oscillation perturbation, while the protein and dry-mass densities increased.
source: They found cell growth was almost inhibited during the perturbation, while the protein and dry-mass densities increased.
evidence: Experimental observation from Knapp et al., 2019.

claim: Cells grew unusually fast after the osmotic oscillation was removed and reached their maximum growth rate about 20 min after the end of the osmotic oscillation.
source: Surprisingly, cells grew unusually fast after the osmotic oscillation was removed and reached their maximum growth rate about 20 min after the end of the osmotic oscillation.
evidence: Experimental observation from Knapp et al., 2019.

claim: The maximum growth rate after osmotic oscillation can be twice the growth rate in the reference growth medium.
source: The maximum growth rate can be twice the growth rate in the reference growth medium, and the elevation in growth rate can persist for two to three cell cycles.
evidence: Experimental observation from Knapp et al., 2019.

claim: The elevation in growth rate after osmotic oscillation can persist for two to three cell cycles.
source: The maximum growth rate can be twice the growth rate in the reference growth medium, and the elevation in growth rate can persist for two to three cell cycles.
evidence: Experimental observation from Knapp et al., 2019.

claim: The model successfully recapitulates the supergrowth phase and the gradually increasing protein density and dry-mass density during the perturbation.
source: Intriguingly, our model successfully recapitulates the supergrowth phase and the gradually increasing protein density and dry-mass density during the perturbation (Figure 4).
evidence: Model predictions shown in Figure 4 match experimental observations.

claim: Cell-wall synthesis regulation is crucial for the emergence of the supergrowth phase since unwalled cells do not exhibit supergrowth after periodic perturbation.
source: We confirm that cell-wall synthesis regulation is crucial for the emergence of the supergrowth phase since unwalled cells do not exhibit supergrowth after periodic perturbation (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: Model prediction shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: An infinitely long periodic osmotic shock can be equivalently mapped to a constant osmotic shock.
source: Interestingly, we find that an infinitely long periodic osmotic shock can be equivalently mapped to a constant osmotic shock (see the detailed discussions and proof in Section D of Appendix 1)
evidence: Theoretical result derived in appendix.

claim: Infinitely long periodic osmotic shock and constant osmotic shock have the same time-averaged growth rate and protein density in the steady states.
source: Interestingly, we find that an infinitely long periodic osmotic shock can be equivalently mapped to a constant osmotic shock (see the detailed discussions and proof in Section D of Appendix 1), which means that they have the same time-averaged growth rate and protein density in the steady states (Appendix 1—figure 2F).
evidence: Theoretical result shown in Appendix 1—figure 2F.

claim: The predicted growth rate peaks vs. the period length and number of periods quantitatively match the experimental data without any further fitting.
source: As a strong support of our model, our predictions quantitatively match the experimental data without any further fitting.
evidence: Model predictions match experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Switching from a long hyperosmotic period to the reference growth medium is equivalent to a constant hypoosmotic shock.
source: Therefore, switching from a long hyperosmotic period to the reference growth medium is equivalent to a constant hypoosmotic shock, where we have shown that the growth rate peak increases with the amplitude (Figure 3E).
evidence: Inference from model dynamics with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Beyond the critical amplitude at the kink point, the cytoplasm is completely jammed during the hyperosmotic shock such that the cell states are precisely the same before and after the hyperosmotic shock.
source: However, the crowding effect becomes more pronounced as the amplitude increases. Beyond the critical amplitude at the kink point, the cytoplasm is completely jammed during the hyperosmotic shock such that the cell states are precisely the same before and after the hyperosmotic shock, which means no supergrowth phase beyond this critical amplitude.
evidence: Mechanistic explanation based on model dynamics.

claim: The theory captures the steady-state properties of constant turgor pressure and reduced growth rate with increasing external osmolarity.
source: Our theory captures the steady-state properties of constant turgor pressure and reduced growth rate with increasing external osmolarity.
evidence: Summary of model predictions.

claim: The growth rate reduction is due to the loss of free water and subsequent intracellular crowding as the external osmolarity increases.
source: We remark that the growth rate reduction is due to the loss of free water and subsequent intracellular crowding as the external osmolarity increases.
evidence: Mechanistic explanation from model.

claim: The theory predicts a critical external osmolarity above which cell growth is completely inhibited.
source: In particular, we predict a critical external osmolarity above which cell growth is completely inhibited and a universal relationship between the normalized growth rate and the normalized internal osmotic pressure, fitting the data of bacteria and yeast.
evidence: Model prediction validated by experimental data.

claim: There is a universal relationship between the normalized growth rate and the normalized internal osmotic pressure, fitting the data of bacteria and yeast.
source: In particular, we predict a critical external osmolarity above which cell growth is completely inhibited and a universal relationship between the normalized growth rate and the normalized internal osmotic pressure, fitting the data of bacteria and yeast.

claim: Cells defective in osmoregulation cannot grow even if the external osmolarity is only mildly higher than the reference value.
source: Cells defective in osmoregulation cannot grow even if the external osmolarity is only mildly higher than the reference value.

source: Cells defective in cell-wall synthesis regulation cannot maintain turgor pressure as the external osmolarity increases, even though they grow faster than WT cells (Figure 2B), which will be a strong support of our theory if confirmed by experiments.

claim: The model predicts a non-monotonic time dependence of protein density after a constant hyperosmotic shock.
source: Regarding dynamic behaviors, our model predicts a non-monotonic time dependence of protein density after a constant hyperosmotic shock.
evidence: Model prediction.

claim: The predicted growth rate peaks quantitatively agree with the experimental data without additional fitting.
source: As a strong support of our theory, the predicted growth rate peaks quantitatively agree with the experimental data without additional fitting.
evidence: Quantitative comparison between model predictions and experimental data.

claim: Cell-wall synthesis regulation plays a critical role in the supergrowth phenomenon.
source: We demonstrate the critical role of cell-wall synthesis regulation in the supergrowth phenomenon (Section E of Appendix 1).
evidence: Demonstrated through model analysis in appendix.

claim: Knapp et al., 2019, observed the rapid repolarization of the cell-wall glucan synthase Bgs4 to the cell tip following the removal of osmotic oscillations in fission yeast.
source: Knapp et al., 2019, observed the rapid repolarization of the cell-wall glucan synthase Bgs4 to the cell tip following the removal of osmotic oscillations in fission yeast, in agreement with the dynamics of the cell-wall synthesis efficiency predicted from our model (compare Figure 4—figure supplement 1 in this work and Figure S4H in Knapp et al., 2019).

claim: The rapid repolarization of Bgs4 is in agreement with the dynamics of the cell-wall synthesis efficiency predicted from the model.
source: Knapp et al., 2019, observed the rapid repolarization of the cell-wall glucan synthase Bgs4 to the cell tip following the removal of osmotic oscillations in fission yeast, in agreement with the dynamics of the cell-wall synthesis efficiency predicted from our model (compare Figure 4—figure supplement 1 in this work and Figure S4H in Knapp et al., 2019).

claim: The model is intrinsically a coarse-grained model with many molecular details regarding gene expression regulation neglected.
source: We remark that our model is intrinsically a coarse-grained model with many molecular details regarding gene expression regulation neglected, which allows us to gain more analytical insights.

source: Shen et al., 2023, studied the responses to osmotic stress in glucose-limited environments and found that cells exhibited stronger osmotic gene expression response under glucose-limited conditions than under glucose-rich conditions.
